title: "Consequences for People and Places"
description: "What does climate action change, for whom, where and over what period?"
canonical-url: "/research/consequences-for-people-and-places.html"
---

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_site.py; do not edit. -->

Climate action changes more than greenhouse-gas emissions. It may alter health, affordability, mobility, employment, social cohesion, local economies, public services and exposure to risk. Yet appraisal often reports average benefits or total economic value, obscuring whether the same action produces different consequences across neighbourhoods, populations and periods.

Consequences for People and Places examines benefits, co-costs, burdens, adverse effects, trade-offs and distributional change. It asks who gains, who pays, where effects occur, how they develop over time and which consequences remain outside conventional appraisal. It also examines how delivery arrangements shape these outcomes. Consequences complete the learning cycle because they test prior assumptions, reveal unanticipated inequalities and change what other cities may plausibly infer from the intervention.

::: {.what-this-changes}
**The proposition.** An intervention’s climate value cannot be separated from the distribution, timing and location of its wider consequences.
:::

**What this theme does not assume.** Consequences include intended and unintended effects, benefits and harms, and outcomes that cannot be reduced to a single monetary measure. The theme does not presume that climate action is automatically equitable or locally beneficial.

A package that appears equitable policy by policy may produce concentrated cumulative burdens or benefits.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Integrated household microsimulation and geospatial policy-package scenarios could estimate cumulative incidence and identify combinations that amplify or offset burdens.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>integrated microsimulation</li><li>geospatial incidence analysis</li><li>policy-package modelling</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Policy appraisers assessing interacting household and neighbourhood effects.</p></article><article class="idea-card signature-idea" data-narrative-tier="signature"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Delivery-contingent co-benefits</h3><p class="idea-question">Which wider benefits depend on how an intervention is delivered rather than on the intervention alone?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Two cities may adopt the same technology but produce different employment, health, affordability or cohesion outcomes because procurement, ownership, participation and financing differ. Static appraisal can misrepresent who ultimately gains or bears costs when the distribution of consequences changes across implementation stages.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Longitudinal microsimulation and cohort analysis, supported by linked administrative or household data, could examine how incidence changes over time.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>longitudinal microsimulation</li><li>cohort analysis</li><li>linked administrative data</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Policy appraisers examining how incidence changes over time.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Climate action and social cohesion</h3><p class="idea-question">Under which conditions does climate action strengthen trust and collective capacity, and when does perceived unfairness erode them?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Social cohesion is often treated as a background condition for climate action rather than a consequence that policy itself can build or damage. Policies that alter trust, reciprocity or collective capacity may affect both social outcomes and the durability of later climate action.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Panel surveys, social-network measures and natural or quasi-experimental variation in programme exposure could be combined with comparative neighbourhood case studies.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>panel surveys</li><li>social-network analysis</li><li>natural experiments</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Municipal programme designers considering trust and collective capacity.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Where benefits stay and burdens move</h3><p class="idea-question">When do urban climate investments retain employment, income, ownership and health benefits locally, and when do they shift costs or risks elsewhere?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>A programme may appear locally beneficial while relying on distant labour, extractive supply chains or displaced environmental and social burdens. Appraisal boundaries can make local gains visible while hiding consequences outside the city.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Multi-regional input–output analysis, supply-chain tracing, ownership mapping and geospatial incidence analysis could connect local outcomes to consequences elsewhere.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>multi-regional input–output analysis</li><li>supply-chain tracing</li><li>ownership mapping</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Policy appraisers defining geographical and supply-chain boundaries.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Appraising what cannot be priced</h3><p class="idea-question">How should urban climate appraisal represent adverse effects, deep uncertainty and outcomes that resist credible monetisation?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Excluding difficult-to-price outcomes can make analysis appear more precise while systematically omitting effects that communities or decision-makers consider consequential. Appraisal methods shape which consequences enter a decision and which are rendered invisible.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Probabilistic sensitivity analysis, robust decision-making, multi-criteria appraisal and deliberative valuation could be compared to determine what each reveals or conceals.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>probabilistic sensitivity analysis</li><li>robust decision-making</li><li>multi-criteria appraisal</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Policy appraisers working with consequences that resist monetisation.</p></article></div>

## How this connects

- **Input from [Modes of Climate Delivery](/research/modes-of-climate-delivery.html):** Delivery arrangements shape which consequences occur, who experiences them and whether climate action can be maintained over time.
- **Next stage — [Geographies of Climate Learning](/research/geographies-of-climate-learning.html):** Observed consequences generate new knowledge, expose the limits of earlier assumptions and change what other cities may plausibly learn.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
